Holly Dagres (@hdagres)

I’m seeing a lot of misinformation and disinformation about the status of the internet in Iran 🛜 

This thread will unpack all of it:



— https://nitter.net/hdagres/status/2046667949965008939#m

To understand the importance of the internet and social media in Iran for ordinary Iranians, and why the Islamic Republic views it as a national security threat since the 2009 Green Movement, read my report: atlanticcouncil.org/in-depth…

Bottom line: limited signals of connectivity ≠ meaningful restoration of internet access in Iran.

Iranians are finding ways to communicate but they aren’t connected to the world like they used to be.

Don’t forget: Internet access is a human right!

It’s also important to separate this from Iran’s domestic internet. Basic services like banking, ride-hailing, and food delivery are still functioning.

But for the 11+ million business owners relying on Instagram, the situation is devastating. 

See what this Iran-based journalist said on the matter:


زهرا کشوری (@zahrakeshvari)

در این  جنگ خیلی ها بیکار شدند. اقتصاد دیجیتال کاملا نابود شد. بسیاری از کسب و کارهای خرد روستایی و شهرهای کوچک وابسته به اینترنت است. بسیاری از زنان سرپرست خانوار با

Re content producers in Iran, they’re either extremely patient as the shady VPNs aren’t giving consistent connectivity or the individual has been given a white SIM, as is the case with whitelisted Iranian journalists and analysts, and, of course, Explosive Media, the team behind the Lego videos.

Iranians are now buying expensive VPNs from questionable dealers (often built through access to government access tiered internet), with many spending most of their monthly income for small amounts of gigabytes of access.

There’s also 50k-60k Starlink terminal users in Iran, using smuggled kits but there’s currently a major crackdown with those arrested being accused of espionage on behalf of the US and Israel.

Starlink is why all these videos popped up during the state-imposed shutdown in January in response to the anti-regime protests. The blackout was used to cover the unprecedented massacre.

Here’s what Iran-based journalist Elahe Mohammadi, who reported on the funeral of Mahsa Jina Amini and was imprisoned for it, wrote on the issue:


elahemohammadi (@elahe_mohamadii)

دیروز بعد از پنجاه و نمی‌دانم چند روز، گوگل آن هم نصفه‌جان و به زور وصل شد. خبرش سریع بین همه پیچید؛ عده‌ای خوشحال بودند که شاید این نشانه‌ باز شدن بقیه محدودیت‌ها باشد.

اما چند لحظه بعد آدم به خودش می‌آید که: چطور کار به جایی رسیده که مردم باید برای وصل شدن ناقصِ گوگل ذوق کنند؟ برای باز شدن چند لینک ساده، برای ابت

That being said, there’s been bumps of connectivity and now Iranians can use the Google search engine, which started in April.

From @Cloudflare:

:NOTE: The colored area from February 28 until now reflects what is technically assessed as an “outage”.)

Since the war began on February 28, Iran is experiencing the world’s longest state-imposed internet shutdown to date—and also its fifth major shutdown.

Here’s what it looks like:

📵 The #Iran internet blackout is now in its 53rd day after 1248 hours of disconnection from global networks. As authorities work to develop tiered access for select users and businesses, the human impacts and economic harms of this digital censorship measure continue to spiral.
